issues.description: The solution implementation declares lecture attributes using snake_case names (e.g. lecture_name, number_of_inscribed_students) but the constructor, getters/setters, and other methods use camelCase names (e.g. lectureName, numberOfInscribedStudents). This naming mismatch means the solution code references fields that do not exist and will not compile, and it deviates from the UML/description which uses camelCase attribute names.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the field names in the solution consistent with the UML and the rest of the code by using camelCase attribute names (lectureName, numberOfInscribedStudents, numberOfGuestStudents, numberOfLecturers, numberOfTutors). Alternatively, update all usages (constructor, getters/setters, methods) to consistently use the snake_case names — but prefer matching the UML/camelCase naming to avoid confusion.

issues.description: The problem statement UML and the template expect attribute names in camelCase (lectureName, numberOfInscribedStudents, numberOfGuestStudents, numberOfLecturers, numberOfTutors), but the solution's Lecture class declares those fields using snake_case (lecture_name, number_of_inscribed_students, number_of_guest_students, number_of_lecturers, number_of_tutors) while its constructor and methods use the camelCase identifiers. This contradictory naming for the same conceptual attributes creates mapping confusion for students and can lead to compilation/understanding issues.
issues.suggestedFix: Align identifier naming across artifacts. Rename the solution's field declarations to use the camelCase names from the UML (lectureName, numberOfInscribedStudents, numberOfGuestStudents, numberOfLecturers, numberOfTutors) and ensure all constructor parameters and methods reference those same field names. Alternatively, if a different naming convention is desired, update the UML and template to match consistently, but prefer camelCase to follow Java conventions.
